lessons.content:
WHAT IS THE CTS CERTIFICATION?

The Certified Technology Specialist (CTS) credential is the globally recognized benchmark for audiovisual professionals. Administered by AVIXA (the Audiovisual and Integrated Experience Association), the CTS validates that a professional possesses the broad foundational knowledge required to work effectively in the AV industry. Whether you are an AV technician, project manager, sales engineer, or system designer, the CTS demonstrates competence across the entire AV lifecycle.

The CTS is vendor-neutral — it does not test on specific manufacturer products. Instead, it focuses on principles, standards, best practices, and problem-solving skills that apply across all AV environments.

EXAM FORMAT AND LOGISTICS

The CTS exam consists of 100 scored multiple-choice questions. You have 150 minutes (2 hours and 30 minutes) to complete the exam. In addition to the 100 scored items, there are approximately 10 unscored pilot questions mixed in — you will not know which questions are scored and which are pilot, so treat every question as if it counts.

Scoring uses a scaled system ranging from 100 to 500. The passing score is 350 out of 500. This is NOT a simple percentage — a scaled score of 350 does not mean you need exactly 70% correct. The scaling algorithm accounts for difficulty variations between exam versions.

The exam is administered at Pearson VUE testing centers worldwide. You may also take it at AVIXA events like InfoComm. Computer-based testing with on-screen tools including a calculator, a highlight feature, and the ability to flag questions for review.

THE FOUR EXAM DOMAINS

Domain 1: Creating AV Solutions — 35% (approximately 35 questions)
This is the largest domain. It covers needs analysis, site surveys, system design, equipment selection, signal flow, and AV math. If you are going to invest extra study time, this domain gives you the most return.

Domain 2: Operating AV Solutions — 20% (approximately 20 questions)
Covers operating AV equipment, user training, system operation procedures, and troubleshooting from an operator perspective. This includes audio mixing, video switching, control system operation, and presentation support.

Domain 3: Managing AV Solutions Projects — 30% (approximately 30 questions)
The second-largest domain covers project management, documentation, drawings, specifications, budgeting, scheduling, coordination with trades, and project delivery. Many candidates underestimate this domain.

Domain 4: Servicing AV Solutions — 15% (approximately 15 questions)
Covers maintenance, troubleshooting methodology, warranty management, service contracts, and keeping systems operational over their lifecycle.

STUDY STRATEGY: WEIGHT YOUR EFFORT

Your study time should be proportional to domain weights. For every 10 hours of study:
- 3.5 hours on Creating AV Solutions (Domain 1)
- 3.0 hours on Managing Projects (Domain 3)
- 2.0 hours on Operating Solutions (Domain 2)
- 1.5 hours on Servicing Solutions (Domain 4)

CTS VS. CTS-D VS. CTS-I

The CTS is the foundational credential. CTS-D (Design) and CTS-I (Installation) are specialty certifications that build on top of CTS. You must hold a valid CTS before pursuing either specialty. CTS-D focuses on system design, documentation, and coordination with allied professionals. CTS-I focuses on installation, commissioning, and verification. Many AV professionals hold CTS plus one or both specialties.

MAINTAINING YOUR CERTIFICATION

CTS certification is valid for 3 years. To renew, you must earn 30 Renewal Units (RUs) during that 3-year cycle. RUs can be earned through AVIXA-approved training, attending InfoComm or regional events, completing manufacturer training, teaching AV courses, publishing AV content, or participating in AVIXA committees. If you let your certification lapse, you must retake the exam.

EXAM DAY TIPS

1. Arrive 15 minutes early — Pearson VUE requires check-in with valid government ID
2. You cannot bring notes, phones, or personal items into the testing room
3. A calculator is provided on screen — you do NOT need to bring one
4. A formula reference sheet is available during the exam — you do not need to memorize formulas, but you MUST know when and how to apply them
5. Answer every question — there is no penalty for guessing
6. Use a 3-pass approach: First pass answers questions you know immediately, second pass tackles flagged questions with more thought, third pass reviews all answers
7. Budget approximately 90 seconds per question on your first pass

scenarios.situation: A colleague with 3 years of AV experience asks whether they should take the CTS or jump straight to the CTS-D.
scenarios.notice: CTS is a prerequisite for both CTS-D and CTS-I. There is no shortcut to the specialty certifications.
scenarios.nextStep: Advise them to take CTS first, then pursue CTS-D after gaining design-specific experience. The CTS foundational knowledge also helps on the specialty exams.
scenarios.whyMatters: Understanding the certification hierarchy prevents wasted registration fees and failed attempts. CTS-D and CTS-I assume CTS-level knowledge as a baseline.

scenarios.situation: You are planning your CTS study schedule with 6 weeks until your exam date.
scenarios.notice: With 6 weeks and four domains, study time must be allocated strategically based on domain weights, not equally.
scenarios.nextStep: Allocate roughly 2 weeks to Domain 1 (Creating), 2 weeks to Domain 3 (Managing), 1 week to Domain 2 (Operating), and 1 week to Domain 4 (Servicing). Adjust based on your existing strengths.
scenarios.whyMatters: Domain 1 and Domain 3 together account for 65% of the exam. Spending equal time on all four domains leaves points on the table.

lessons.examRelevance: While no exam questions directly ask about exam format, understanding domain weights is critical for efficient preparation. Domains 1 and 3 together represent 65% of the exam — candidates who allocate study time proportionally consistently outperform those who study all areas equally.

lessons.title: The AV Industry: Markets, Systems & Career Paths
lessons.module: Day 1: CTS Foundations, Standards & AV Math
lessons.overview: Explore the professional audiovisual industry landscape, including the types of AV systems deployed across market verticals, career paths available to AV professionals, and the convergence of AV and IT that is reshaping the industry.
learningObjectives: Identify the major market verticals served by the professional AV industry
Describe the core components that make up an AV system and how they interconnect
Explain the convergence of AV and IT and its impact on system design and deployment
Recognize the range of career paths available within the AV industry
Differentiate between residential, commercial, and live event AV applications

keyTerms.definition: Audiovisual systems designed for commercial, institutional, and public use — distinct from consumer/residential AV. Professional AV emphasizes reliability, scalability, manageability, and integration with building systems.
The merging of audiovisual and information technology disciplines as AV systems increasingly use IP networks, IT protocols, and cloud services for signal transport, control, and management.
Integration of multiple communication tools — voice, video, messaging, conferencing, and collaboration — into a single platform, typically delivered over IP networks.
Electronically controlled display systems that show content such as information, advertising, wayfinding, or emergency notifications in public spaces.
A company that designs, installs, programs, and commissions AV systems by combining components from multiple manufacturers into a complete solution. Also known as an AV integrator.
A specific industry sector served by AV professionals, such as corporate, education, government, healthcare, hospitality, worship, or entertainment.
The hardware and software that allows users to operate AV equipment through simplified interfaces like touch panels, keypads, or mobile apps rather than interacting with individual devices.
The path audio, video, and control signals travel from their source through processing and distribution to their destination outputs.

lessons.content:
WHAT DO AV SYSTEMS DO?

At their core, professional audiovisual systems enable communication. They allow people to see, hear, and share information effectively in spaces ranging from small huddle rooms to massive stadiums. Every AV system, regardless of complexity, consists of four fundamental functional blocks:

1. Sources — devices that originate content (laptops, cameras, media players, microphones, document cameras)
2. Signal Processing — devices that manipulate signals (audio DSPs, video scalers, matrix switchers, codecs)
3. Distribution — the infrastructure that moves signals (cables, connectors, network switches, wireless transmitters)
4. Output — devices that present content to humans (displays, projectors, speakers, headphones)

A fifth functional element — Control — ties everything together by allowing users to operate the system through simplified interfaces.

MARKET VERTICALS

The professional AV industry serves distinct market sectors, each with unique requirements:

Corporate: The largest AV market segment. Includes boardrooms, conference rooms, huddle spaces, training centers, executive briefing centers, lobbies, and all-hands meeting spaces. Driven by collaboration and unified communications. Key trends: BYOD (bring your own device), wireless presentation, video conferencing, and room scheduling.

Education: K-12 classrooms, university lecture halls, distance learning labs, and administrative spaces. Emphasis on interactive displays, lecture capture, classroom audio reinforcement, and remote learning platforms. ADA compliance is critical.

Government and Military: Council chambers, courtrooms, command centers, legislative floors, and secure facilities. Requirements include ADA compliance, assistive listening, voting systems, evidence display, and often SCIF-level security for classified environments.

Healthcare: Operating rooms, patient rooms, telemedicine suites, diagnostic imaging review, and medical training facilities. Hygiene, infection control, and HIPAA compliance influence equipment selection. Surgical AV and medical-grade displays are specialized sub-markets.

Hospitality: Hotels, casinos, restaurants, and entertainment venues. Lobbies, ballrooms, convention centers, and guest rooms. Systems must be attractive, intuitive, and reliable with high uptime requirements.

Worship: Houses of worship of all sizes. Audio reinforcement, video projection/IMAG (image magnification), live streaming, lighting, and recording. Volunteer-operated systems must be extremely user-friendly.

Entertainment and Live Events: Concert venues, theaters, theme parks, and touring productions. High-performance audio, large-format projection, LED walls, lighting integration, and show control. Often involves rental and staging companies.

Transportation: Airports, train stations, and transit hubs. Paging systems, flight/arrival information displays, wayfinding, and emergency notification. Reliability and intelligibility are paramount.

AV AND IT CONVERGENCE

The most significant shift in the AV industry over the past two decades is the convergence with information technology. Historically, AV signals traveled over dedicated analog cables — VGA for video, speaker wire for audio, serial cables for control. Today, nearly everything runs over IP networks:

- AV-over-IP replaces point-to-point matrix switches with networked encoders and decoders
- Dante and AES67 transport audio over standard Ethernet
- Control systems communicate via TCP/IP instead of RS-232 serial
- Cloud-based platforms manage and monitor AV systems remotely
- Video conferencing (Teams, Zoom, Webex) has made UC the dominant AV use case

This convergence means AV professionals must understand networking fundamentals — IP addressing, VLANs, QoS, PoE, multicast, and network security. The days of AV being a standalone discipline are over.

CAREER PATHS IN AV

The AV industry offers diverse career paths:

- AV Technician / Installer: Hands-on installation, cable pulling, termination, equipment mounting, and system testing
- AV Programmer: Programming control systems (Crestron, Extron, AMX/Harman), DSP configuration, and system commissioning
- AV Designer: System design, equipment selection, documentation, and coordination with architects and engineers (CTS-D path)
- AV Project Manager: Managing AV projects from scope through closeout, budgets, schedules, and team coordination
- AV Sales / Account Manager: Consultative sales, proposal development, and client relationship management
- AV Consultant: Independent design professionals who create AV designs and specifications for clients without selling equipment
- AV Operations / Support: Operating and maintaining AV systems in corporate, education, or entertainment environments
- Field Service Engineer: Troubleshooting and repairing AV systems, preventive maintenance, and client training

THE ROLE OF THE SYSTEM INTEGRATOR

Most professional AV systems are designed, installed, and commissioned by system integrators (also called AV integrators). These companies employ designers, project managers, programmers, and technicians. They take a client's requirements, design a system, procure equipment from manufacturers and distributors, install and program the system, and hand it over to the client. Integrators are the backbone of the AV industry.

Consultants and integrators serve different roles: consultants design and specify systems independently (they do not sell equipment), while integrators both design and install. Some projects use a consultant-designed, integrator-installed model similar to how architects design buildings that contractors build.

scenarios.situation: A healthcare facility wants AV in their new surgical suite but insists on using the same consumer TV they saw at a big-box store.
scenarios.notice: Consumer displays are not rated for healthcare environments. Medical-grade displays have specific brightness, color accuracy, and hygiene standards. Consumer TVs also lack the 24/7 duty cycle rating needed for healthcare.
scenarios.nextStep: Explain the functional differences: medical-grade displays support DICOM calibration for diagnostic accuracy, have antimicrobial housings, and are rated for continuous operation. Recommend a professional healthcare display.
scenarios.whyMatters: Understanding market vertical requirements prevents inappropriate equipment selection. On the CTS exam, selecting the right equipment for the environment is a core Domain 1 skill.

scenarios.situation: Your company's IT department wants to take over management of all AV systems since 'everything is on the network now.'
scenarios.notice: AV/IT convergence means collaboration is essential, but AV systems have unique requirements that IT teams may not fully understand — such as multicast traffic management, low-latency switching, and real-time media transport.
scenarios.nextStep: Propose a collaborative model where AV and IT teams share responsibility. AV manages system design, programming, and user experience; IT manages network infrastructure, security policies, and monitoring.
scenarios.whyMatters: The CTS exam tests understanding of AV/IT convergence. The correct answer is always collaboration between AV and IT, not one team replacing the other.

lessons.examRelevance: The CTS exam expects you to understand the breadth of AV applications and market verticals. Questions may present a scenario in a specific vertical and ask you to identify the most appropriate system type or design consideration. Understanding AV/IT convergence is tested across multiple domains.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which market vertical typically requires the MOST user-friendly operation because systems are often run by volunteers?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Houses of worship frequently rely on volunteers with minimal technical training to operate AV systems. This makes ease of use and simplified control interfaces critical design requirements.

knowledgeCheck.question: What are the four fundamental functional blocks of any AV system?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Every AV system follows the signal chain from Sources (content origination) through Signal Processing (manipulation) and Distribution (transport) to Output (presentation to users). Control is the fifth element that ties them together.

memorize: Four functional blocks: Sources → Signal Processing → Distribution → Output (plus Control)
Major market verticals: Corporate, Education, Government, Healthcare, Hospitality, Worship, Entertainment, Transportation
understand: AV/IT convergence is a collaboration, not a takeover by either side
System integrators design, install, and commission — consultants design and specify without selling equipment
Each market vertical has unique requirements that drive design decisions
practice: For each market vertical, list 2-3 unique AV requirements that differentiate it from others
examTraps: Don't confuse consumer AV products with professional AV — the exam is about professional/commercial systems
AV/IT convergence questions always favor collaboration, never one team dominating the other
studyNotes.fieldTip: Corporate AV is the largest market segment, but specializing in a niche vertical like healthcare or government can command premium rates because of the specialized knowledge required.

lessons.summary: The professional AV industry serves diverse market verticals including corporate, education, government, healthcare, hospitality, worship, and entertainment. Every AV system consists of four functional blocks — Sources, Signal Processing, Distribution, and Output — tied together by Control. AV/IT convergence is transforming the industry as IP networks replace dedicated AV cabling. Career paths range from installation technicians to designers, consultants, and project managers.

lessons.content:
AVIXA STANDARDS OVERVIEW

AVIXA develops ANSI-accredited standards that define best practices for AV system design, installation, and documentation. These standards are not just guidelines — they represent the industry consensus on professional practice. The CTS exam tests your knowledge of these standards heavily, particularly their purpose and application.

DISPLAY IMAGE SIZE — ANSI/AVIXA V202.01 (DISCAS)

The Display Image Size for 2D Content in Audiovisual Systems standard replaced the older informal 4H/6H/8H guidelines with a more rigorous approach to display sizing. DISCAS categorizes content into types based on the detail level required:

- Basic Decision Making (BDM): Large text, simple graphics, video. The farthest viewer can be up to 8 times the image height (8H) from the screen.
- Basic Analytical Decision Making (BADM): Spreadsheets, detailed graphics. Maximum viewing distance of 6H.
- Analytical Decision Making (ADM): Fine detail, small text, complex data. Maximum viewing distance of 4H.
- Forensic/Inspection: Pixel-level examination. Maximum viewing distance of 2H.

The key concept: as content becomes more detailed, viewers must be closer to the screen (or the screen must be larger). For the CTS exam, understand that DISCAS drives display sizing based on content type and farthest viewer distance.

DISPLAY CONTRAST — ANSI/AVIXA V201.01

This standard addresses display readability in real-world lighting conditions. A display's contrast ratio in a dark room (native contrast) is very different from its effective contrast in a brightly lit conference room. The standard defines minimum contrast ratios based on ambient light:

- Projected images in high-ambient-light rooms may fail to achieve adequate contrast
- Direct-view displays (LCD, LED) maintain better contrast in bright environments
- Screen gain, display brightness (nits/lumens), and ambient light all factor into the calculation

AUDIO COVERAGE — ANSI/AVIXA A102.01

The audio coverage uniformity standard specifies that in a properly designed audio reinforcement system, sound pressure levels (SPL) should not vary by more than ±3 dB across the intended listening area. This means every seat in the audience should receive essentially the same audio level. The standard applies to speech reinforcement — the most common AV audio application.

Key design implications:
- Ceiling speaker spacing and coverage angles must be calculated to achieve uniform coverage
- Edge-of-coverage overlap between adjacent speakers should be designed to maintain ±3 dB uniformity
- Proper speaker selection, placement, and DSP configuration are required to meet this standard

DOCUMENTATION — ANSI/AVIXA D401.01

This standard defines what documentation must be delivered with an AV system. Required documentation includes:
- As-built drawings reflecting the actual installed system (not just the design drawings)
- Equipment lists with model numbers, serial numbers, and locations
- System operation guides written for the actual end users
- Maintenance procedures and schedules
- Cable schedules matching installed labels
- Network configuration documentation
- Warranty information and vendor contacts

CABLE LABELING — ANSI/AVIXA F501.01

Every cable in an AV system must be labeled at both ends with a unique identifier that matches the system documentation. Labels must be:
- Machine-printed (not handwritten)
- Durable enough to remain legible for the life of the system
- Applied within 12 inches of the termination point
- Consistent in format throughout the project
- Matched to cable schedules and as-built drawings

Proper labeling saves enormous time during troubleshooting and maintenance. A cable you cannot identify is a cable you cannot service.

RACK BUILDING — ANSI/AVIXA F502.02

The rack building standard covers professional equipment rack assembly:
- Equipment mounting: 1 RU (rack unit) = 1.75 inches. Standard racks are 42 RU (73.5 inches of usable space)
- Ventilation: adequate airflow with proper spacing, blanking panels for unused spaces
- Cable management: organized cable routing, service loops, horizontal and vertical cable managers
- Grounding: single-point ground for each rack connected to building ground
- Accessibility: rear access for maintenance, adequate clearance on all sides
- Weight distribution: heavier equipment at bottom, power distribution at bottom or top per design
- Labeling: all equipment and cables labeled per F501.01

BUILDING CODES AND REGULATIONS

National Electrical Code (NEC/NFPA 70):
- Plenum-rated cables (CMP) required in air-handling spaces above drop ceilings
- Riser-rated cables (CMR) for vertical runs between floors
- Conduit fill limited to 40% for multiple cables in a single conduit
- Circuit breaker sizing must account for total connected load with 80% continuous load rule
- All electrical work must comply with local amendments to the NEC

ADA (Americans with Disabilities Act):
- Assistive listening systems required in assembly areas with audio reinforcement
- User interface controls mounted between 15 and 48 inches AFF (above finished floor)
- Visual notification devices (strobes) required in addition to audible alarms
- Captioning capability for public-facing video content
- Accessible routes to AV operator positions

Fire and Life Safety:
- AV equipment cannot obstruct exits, fire alarm devices, or sprinkler heads
- Projector mounting must meet seismic requirements in applicable zones
- Display mounting must use safety cables or approved mounting systems rated for the weight

AVIXA CODE OF ETHICS

All CTS holders are bound by the AVIXA Code of Ethics:
1. Honesty: Represent qualifications and experience truthfully
2. Competence: Only undertake work within your area of competence
3. Confidentiality: Protect client proprietary and confidential information
4. Safety: Never compromise safety for cost or schedule
5. Conflicts of Interest: Disclose any conflicts that could influence professional judgment
6. Professional Development: Maintain current knowledge through continuing education
7. Respect: Treat colleagues, clients, and all stakeholders with respect

Violation of the Code of Ethics can result in revocation of CTS certification.

scenarios.situation: An installer wants to use standard CM-rated (general purpose) cables in the plenum space above the drop ceiling to save money.
scenarios.notice: The NEC requires plenum-rated (CMP) cables in air-handling spaces. Using CM-rated cables in a plenum is a code violation that creates a fire and safety hazard.
scenarios.nextStep: Require CMP-rated cables for all runs in the plenum space. The cost difference is modest compared to the safety risk and code compliance requirement.
scenarios.whyMatters: Plenum cable requirements appear frequently on the CTS exam. The answer is always CMP in plenum spaces — no exceptions for cost savings.

scenarios.situation: A client wants a touch panel control interface mounted on the wall at 60 inches above the floor in a public building.
scenarios.notice: ADA requires user interface controls to be accessible, typically mounted between 15 and 48 inches above finished floor for forward approach.
scenarios.nextStep: Recommend mounting the touch panel at 48 inches AFF maximum, or provide a secondary accessible control point.
scenarios.whyMatters: ADA compliance is not optional in public buildings. The CTS exam tests your knowledge of accessible mounting heights.

lessons.examRelevance: AVIXA standards appear throughout the CTS exam across all four domains. You must know what each standard addresses (not necessarily every detail within it). Expect questions about DISCAS content categories and viewing distances, ±3 dB audio coverage uniformity, cable labeling requirements, rack building practices, and plenum cable requirements.

knowledgeCheck.question: According to ANSI/AVIXA A102.01, what is the maximum allowable variation in sound pressure level across the listening area?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The AVIXA Audio Coverage Uniformity standard specifies that SPL should not vary more than ±3 dB across the listening area. This ensures all listeners receive essentially equal audio levels.

knowledgeCheck.question: What type of cable rating is required for cables installed in plenum spaces above drop ceilings?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The NEC requires CMP-rated cables in plenum (air-handling) spaces. CMP cables are manufactured with fire-resistant jackets that limit smoke and toxic gas production.

memorize: DISCAS viewing distances: BDM=8H, BADM=6H, ADM=4H
Audio coverage uniformity: ±3 dB per A102.01
1 RU = 1.75 inches, standard rack = 42 RU
Plenum = CMP, Riser = CMR
ADA touch panel height: 15-48 inches AFF
Conduit fill: 40% maximum

Cable labeling at both ends is required by F501.01, not optional
The Code of Ethics is binding — violations can result in certification revocation
practice: Match each AVIXA standard number to its subject: V202.01=display size, V201.01=contrast, A102.01=audio coverage, D401.01=documentation, F501.01=labeling, F502.02=racks

Audio coverage is ±3 dB, not ±6 dB — the tighter tolerance is for speech intelligibility
CMP is for plenum spaces, CMR is for riser (vertical between floors) — don't mix them up
studyNotes.fieldTip: In practice, AVIXA standards are the baseline for quality AV work. Clients and consultants increasingly specify compliance with these standards in their RFPs. Knowing them gives you a competitive edge.

lessons.summary: AVIXA standards define professional AV practice: DISCAS (V202.01) for display sizing by content type, V201.01 for contrast, A102.01 for ±3 dB audio coverage uniformity, D401.01 for documentation, F501.01 for cable labeling, and F502.02 for rack building. Building codes require CMP cables in plenum spaces and ADA-compliant mounting heights. The AVIXA Code of Ethics is binding on all CTS holders.
