Apply measurement tools and techniques used in AV site surveys

keyTerms.definition: The standard unit of vertical measurement in equipment racks. 1 RU equals 1.75 inches (44.45 mm). A standard full-height rack provides 42 RU of usable space.
A proportional relationship between dimensions on a drawing and actual dimensions. Common AV scales include 1/4 inch = 1 foot (1:48) and 1/8 inch = 1 foot (1:96).
British Thermal Units per hour — the standard measure of heat output used for HVAC load calculations. AV equipment heat output in BTU/hr = watts × 3.412.
Area measured in square feet (ft²), calculated as length × width. Critical for determining room acoustics, speaker coverage, and display sizing.
Volume measured in cubic feet (ft³), calculated as length × width × height. Used in acoustic calculations including reverberation time (RT60).
The base unit of length in the metric system. 1 meter = 3.281 feet = 39.37 inches. Many AV specifications use metric measurements.
A specialized ruler with multiple scales marked on its edges, used to measure dimensions directly from architectural drawings without manual calculation.

lessons.content:
WHY AV MATH MATTERS

AV professionals use math every day — calculating display sizes, determining speaker coverage, sizing amplifiers, reading blueprints, and ensuring code compliance. The CTS exam includes math-based questions across all four domains. The good news: the formulas are provided on the exam. Your job is to know WHEN to use each formula and HOW to plug in the right values.

UNIT SYSTEMS IN AV

The AV industry uses both US customary and metric units, often in the same project:

US Customary: feet, inches, pounds, Fahrenheit
Metric (SI): meters, centimeters, kilograms, Celsius

Key conversion factors:
- 1 foot = 12 inches = 0.3048 meters
- 1 meter = 3.281 feet = 39.37 inches
- 1 inch = 25.4 millimeters
- 1 pound = 0.4536 kilograms
- Fahrenheit to Celsius: °C = (°F - 32) × 5/9
- Celsius to Fahrenheit: °F = (°C × 9/5) + 32

AREA CALCULATIONS

Area = Length × Width

Area is measured in square feet (ft²) or square meters (m²). You will calculate area for:
- Room floor area for speaker coverage patterns
- Wall area for display placement and sight line analysis
- Screen area for projection brightness calculations

Conversion: 1 m² = 10.764 ft²

For non-rectangular rooms, break the space into rectangles, calculate each area separately, and add them together.

VOLUME CALCULATIONS

Volume = Length × Width × Height

Volume is measured in cubic feet (ft³) or cubic meters (m³). Volume is critical for:
- Acoustic calculations (RT60 reverberation time uses room volume)
- HVAC load calculations (heat dissipation from AV equipment)
- Speaker coverage analysis in three-dimensional spaces

Conversion: 1 m³ = 35.315 ft³

READING ARCHITECTURAL SCALES

Architectural drawings are scaled-down representations of real spaces. The scale tells you the ratio between the drawing and reality.

Common architectural scales for AV work:
- 1/4" = 1'-0" (quarter-inch scale) — most common for floor plans. Every quarter inch on the drawing represents 1 foot in real life. A room that measures 5 inches wide on the drawing is 20 feet wide in reality (5 × 4 = 20).
- 1/8" = 1'-0" (eighth-inch scale) — used for larger floor plans. Every eighth inch = 1 foot. Same room: 2.5 inches on drawing = 20 feet (2.5 × 8 = 20).
- 1/2" = 1'-0" (half-inch scale) — detail drawings. Every half inch = 1 foot.
- 3/8" = 1'-0" — less common but appears on some drawings.

Always check the title block of a drawing for the scale. If a drawing has been printed at a different size than intended, the scale will be wrong — use the graphic scale bar if provided.

RACK UNIT CALCULATIONS

1 RU (Rack Unit) = 1.75 inches

Standard rack sizes:
- 42 RU (full height) = 73.5 inches of usable space (42 × 1.75)
- 25 RU (half height) = 43.75 inches
- 12 RU (desktop/wall mount) = 21 inches

To calculate rack space needed:
1. List all equipment with their RU heights
2. Add ventilation spacing (typically 1 RU between heat-generating devices)
3. Add 1 RU for each patch panel, power strip, or cable management panel
4. Total RU needed + 20% spare capacity = recommended rack size

Overall rack height includes top and bottom frames, adding roughly 6-8 inches beyond the usable RU space.

BTU/HR HEAT CALCULATIONS

AV equipment generates heat. HVAC systems must account for this heat load to maintain proper operating temperatures (typically 64-75°F / 18-24°C).

BTU/hr = Watts × 3.412

To calculate the heat load of an AV rack:
1. Sum the wattage of all equipment in the rack (from manufacturer spec sheets)
2. Multiply by 3.412 to convert to BTU/hr
3. Provide this number to the HVAC engineer

MEASUREMENT TOOLS FOR AV

- Laser distance measure: Accurate room dimensions (±1/16")
- SPL meter: Sound pressure levels in decibels (dB)
- Light meter (lux meter): Ambient light levels for display contrast calculations
- Tape measure: Quick measurements, cable runs
- Scale rule: Reading architectural drawings
- Infrared thermometer: Equipment operating temperatures
- Cable tester: Verifying cable continuity and wiring
- Stud finder: Locating structural support for mounting

scenarios.situation: You are reading a floor plan at 1/4" = 1'-0" scale and need to determine if a 100-inch diagonal display will fit on a wall that measures 2.5 inches on the drawing.
scenarios.notice: At 1/4" scale, 2.5 inches on the drawing = 10 feet in reality (2.5 × 4 = 10 feet = 120 inches). A 100-inch diagonal 16:9 display is approximately 87 inches wide, so it fits on the 120-inch wall.
scenarios.nextStep: Verify the display dimensions from the manufacturer spec sheet and confirm adequate clearance on both sides for mounting hardware and service access.
scenarios.whyMatters: Reading architectural scales correctly is fundamental to AV design. An incorrect scale reading could result in specifying equipment that does not physically fit in the space.

scenarios.situation: The HVAC engineer asks you for the total heat load of your proposed AV rack containing 2,400 watts of equipment.
scenarios.notice: HVAC engineers need heat output in BTU/hr, not watts. The conversion factor is 3.412.
scenarios.nextStep: Calculate: 2,400 watts × 3.412 = 8,189 BTU/hr. Report this value to the HVAC engineer so they can size the cooling system appropriately.
scenarios.whyMatters: If you report watts instead of BTU/hr, or miscalculate the conversion, the HVAC system may be undersized, leading to equipment overheating and failure.

workedExamples.given: A room measures 30 feet long × 20 feet wide × 10 feet high (ceiling).
workedExamples.asked: Calculate the room's floor area in square feet and volume in cubic feet.
workedExamples.solution:
Floor area = Length × Width = 30 × 20 = 600 ft²
Volume = Length × Width × Height = 30 × 20 × 10 = 6,000 ft³
workedExamples.answer: Floor area = 600 ft² and Volume = 6,000 ft³
workedExamples.wrongApproach: A common mistake is calculating volume using only two dimensions (30 × 20 = 600) — that gives you area, not volume. Volume requires all three dimensions.

workedExamples.given: An AV equipment rack contains the following: amplifier (3 RU), DSP processor (1 RU), matrix switcher (2 RU), control processor (1 RU), network switch (1 RU), UPS (2 RU), two patch panels (1 RU each), and one power distribution unit (1 RU).
workedExamples.asked: Calculate the total rack units needed, including 1 RU ventilation space above each heat-generating device (amplifier, DSP, matrix switcher, control processor).
workedExamples.solution:
Equipment: 3 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 13 RU
Ventilation: 4 devices × 1 RU each = 4 RU
Total = 13 + 4 = 17 RU
With 20% spare: 17 × 1.2 = 20.4 → round up to 21 RU minimum
Recommend a 25 RU rack for adequate space.
workedExamples.answer: 17 RU minimum (21 RU with 20% spare capacity), recommend a 25 RU rack
workedExamples.wrongApproach: Forgetting ventilation spacing is a common error. Without ventilation gaps, heat-generating equipment runs hotter, potentially reducing lifespan and reliability.

workedExamples.given: An AV closet contains equipment drawing a total of 1,800 watts.
workedExamples.asked: Calculate the heat output in BTU/hr for the HVAC engineer.
workedExamples.wrongApproach: Using the wrong conversion factor (such as dividing by 3.412 instead of multiplying) would give approximately 527 BTU/hr — drastically underestimating the cooling needed.

lessons.examRelevance: Math questions on the CTS exam provide formulas on a reference sheet, but you must know which formula to apply. Area, volume, rack unit calculations, BTU conversions, and architectural scale reading are all testable. The exam does not test advanced math — it tests practical AV math that you use daily.

knowledgeCheck.question: How many inches is 1 Rack Unit (RU)?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: 1 RU = 1.75 inches (44.45 mm). This is a universally standardized measurement used in all professional equipment racks worldwide.

knowledgeCheck.question: On a floor plan drawn at 1/4 inch = 1 foot scale, a wall measures 3 inches on the drawing. What is the actual wall length?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: At 1/4" = 1'-0" scale, multiply the drawing measurement by 4. 3 inches × 4 = 12 feet.

memorize: 1 RU = 1.75 inches
BTU/hr = Watts × 3.412
1 meter = 3.281 feet
1 inch = 25.4 mm
Standard rack = 42 RU
1/4" = 1'-0" means multiply drawing measurement by 4
understand: Area is 2D (length × width), Volume is 3D (length × width × height)
Always include ventilation spacing when calculating rack requirements
BTU/hr is what HVAC engineers need — not watts
practice: Convert room dimensions between feet and meters
Calculate rack requirements for a list of equipment
Read scaled dimensions from architectural drawings
examTraps: Don't confuse area (ft²) with volume (ft³) — the exam may describe a room and ask for volume when you might reflexively calculate area
BTU/hr = Watts × 3.412 — do NOT divide
At 1/4" scale, multiply by 4, not divide by 4
studyNotes.fieldTip: Always bring a laser distance measure and a scale rule on site surveys. Verify room dimensions yourself — never rely solely on architectural drawings, as as-built conditions frequently differ from plans.

lessons.summary: AV math foundations include unit conversions (1 RU = 1.75", 1 m = 3.281 ft), area calculations (L×W), volume calculations (L×W×H), BTU/hr heat conversion (watts × 3.412), and architectural scale reading (1/4" = 1'-0" means ×4). Standard racks provide 42 RU of space. These calculations appear throughout the CTS exam — know when and how to apply each formula.

lessons.title: AV Math: Ratios, Aspect Ratios & Display Sizing
lessons.module: Day 1: CTS Foundations, Standards & AV Math
lessons.overview: Master the math behind display selection including aspect ratios, AVIXA DISCAS calculations, throw ratio for projectors, converting between diagonal and height/width measurements, and pixel density considerations.
learningObjectives: Calculate display width and height from diagonal measurement and aspect ratio
Apply AVIXA DISCAS guidelines to determine minimum display size for a given room
Calculate projector throw ratio and determine required throw distance or lens selection
Determine appropriate screen size based on farthest viewer distance and content type
Understand pixel density and its relationship to viewing distance

keyTerms.definition: The proportional relationship between a display's width and height. Common ratios: 16:9 (widescreen, most common), 16:10 (productivity), 4:3 (legacy). Expressed as width:height.

Display Image Size for 2D Content in Audiovisual Systems (ANSI/AVIXA V202.01). Defines maximum viewing distances relative to image height: 8H for basic content, 6H for standard business, 4H for analytical, 2H for forensic.

The ratio of a projector's throw distance to the image width it produces. Throw Ratio = Distance to Screen / Image Width. A 1.5:1 throw ratio means the projector must be 1.5 times the image width away from the screen.
The vertical dimension of the displayed image, used as the base unit in DISCAS calculations. All viewing distance limits are expressed as multiples of image height.

A measure of a projection screen's reflectivity relative to a reference surface. Gain of 1.0 is reference (matte white). Higher gain (1.3, 1.5) reflects more light toward viewers but narrows the viewing angle.
Pixels per inch — the number of pixels in a linear inch of display. Higher PPI means finer detail. At closer viewing distances, higher PPI is needed to avoid visible pixels.
The distance from the projector lens to the screen surface. Determined by the projector's throw ratio and the desired image width: Throw Distance = Throw Ratio × Image Width.
The measurement from one corner of a display to the opposite corner. Display sizes are specified by diagonal. To convert: for 16:9, Width ≈ Diagonal × 0.872, Height ≈ Diagonal × 0.490.

lessons.content:
ASPECT RATIOS EXPLAINED

Aspect ratio describes the shape of a display — the relationship between width and height. It is written as width:height.

16:9 — The dominant aspect ratio in professional AV. All HDTV (1080p), 4K (3840×2160), and most content is produced in 16:9. This is the default assumption unless told otherwise.

16:10 — Common on computer monitors oriented toward productivity. Slightly taller than 16:9, providing more vertical space for documents and spreadsheets. WUXGA (1920×1200) is 16:10.

4:3 — Legacy standard from traditional TV and early computer monitors. XGA (1024×768) is 4:3. Still encountered in older systems but rarely specified for new installations.

21:9 (Ultrawide) — Used for cinema content and some specialized collaboration displays. Not common in standard AV installations.

CONVERTING DIAGONAL TO WIDTH AND HEIGHT

Displays are sold by diagonal measurement, but design calculations use width and height. For a 16:9 display:

The relationship uses the Pythagorean theorem. For 16:9:
- Width = Diagonal × 0.8716
- Height = Diagonal × 0.4903

For a 4:3 display:
- Width = Diagonal × 0.8
- Height = Diagonal × 0.6

Example: An 86-inch 16:9 display
- Width = 86 × 0.8716 = 74.96 inches (approximately 75 inches)
- Height = 86 × 0.4903 = 42.17 inches (approximately 42 inches)

DISCAS — DISPLAY SIZING BY CONTENT TYPE

The AVIXA DISCAS standard determines the minimum display size based on what content viewers need to see and how far away they sit.

Content categories and maximum viewing distance (as multiples of image height H):
- Basic Decision Making (BDM): Video, large graphics — max 8H
- Basic Analytical Decision Making (BADM): Standard business content, presentations — max 6H
- Analytical Decision Making (ADM): Spreadsheets, detailed data — max 4H
- Forensic/Inspection: Pixel-level detail — max 2H

To determine minimum display size:
1. Identify the content type (most business applications are BADM = 6H)
2. Measure the farthest viewer distance
3. Calculate minimum image height: H = Farthest Distance / Maximum H-multiplier
4. Convert to diagonal if needed using the aspect ratio

Example: Farthest viewer is 24 feet from the screen, content is standard business (BADM = 6H)
- Minimum H = 24 feet / 6 = 4 feet = 48 inches
- For 16:9: Diagonal = H / 0.4903 = 48 / 0.4903 = 97.9 inches
- Specify at least a 98-inch display or 100-inch screen

PROJECTOR THROW RATIO

Throw ratio determines how far a projector must be from the screen to create a specific image width.

Throw Ratio = Throw Distance / Image Width

Projector categories by throw ratio:
- Ultra-short throw (UST): 0.3:1 to 0.5:1 — projector is very close to the screen
- Short throw: 0.5:1 to 1.0:1 — reduced distance, good for smaller rooms
- Standard throw: 1.0:1 to 2.0:1 — most common
- Long throw: 2.0:1 and above — large venues

To find required throw distance:
Throw Distance = Throw Ratio × Image Width

To find required throw ratio when distance is fixed:
Throw Ratio = Throw Distance / Image Width

Example: You need a 120-inch wide image and the projector must be mounted 18 feet (216 inches) from the screen.
Throw Ratio = 216 / 120 = 1.8:1
Select a projector with a zoom lens range that includes 1.8:1.

PIXEL DENSITY AND VIEWING DISTANCE

Resolution matters in context of viewing distance. A 1080p display viewed from 3 feet looks pixelated; the same display from 15 feet looks sharp. Higher resolution (4K, 8K) is most beneficial when:
- Viewers sit close to the display
- Content contains fine detail (text, spreadsheets, medical imaging)
- Display size is very large

For standard business content at typical conference room distances (8-20 feet), 4K provides a visible improvement over 1080p on displays 65 inches and larger. For displays under 55 inches at distances over 10 feet, 1080p is adequate.

SCREEN GAIN AND AMBIENT LIGHT

Projection screens have a gain rating that affects brightness and viewing angle:
- 1.0 gain (matte white): Equal reflection in all directions. Widest viewing angle. Best for rooms where viewers are spread across a wide area.
- 1.3 gain: Moderate boost to on-axis brightness. Good balance of brightness and viewing angle.
- 1.5+ gain: Significantly brighter on-axis but narrow viewing angle. Best for long, narrow rooms.
- ALR (Ambient Light Rejecting): Special screens designed for bright rooms. They reject off-axis ambient light while reflecting projector light. Typical gain of 0.6-0.8 but with much better contrast in lit rooms.

Higher gain is NOT always better — it narrows the usable viewing angle. For a wide room, a high-gain screen creates hot spots (brighter center, dimmer edges).

scenarios.situation: A client's conference room has the farthest seat 30 feet from the planned display location. They will primarily display spreadsheets and financial data.
scenarios.notice: Spreadsheet and financial data is Analytical Decision Making content (ADM = 4H maximum distance).
scenarios.nextStep: Calculate minimum image height: H = 30 ft / 4 = 7.5 ft = 90 inches. For 16:9: Diagonal = 90 / 0.4903 = 183.6 inches. This is too large for a single flat panel — recommend a projection system or LED video wall with at least a 90-inch image height.
scenarios.whyMatters: Using the wrong DISCAS content category (e.g., BDM at 8H instead of ADM at 4H) would undersize the display, making spreadsheet data unreadable for rear-seat viewers.

scenarios.situation: The architect's ceiling plan shows the projector mount location is 15 feet from the screen wall. You need to produce a 10-foot (120-inch) wide image.
scenarios.notice: The throw distance is fixed at 15 feet (180 inches) and image width is 120 inches.
scenarios.nextStep: Calculate throw ratio: 180 / 120 = 1.5:1. Select a projector with a lens or zoom range that includes 1.5:1 throw ratio.
scenarios.whyMatters: If you select a projector with the wrong throw ratio for the available distance, the image will be the wrong size — either too small or overflowing the screen.

workedExamples.asked: Calculate the display width and height in inches.
workedExamples.solution:
Width = Diagonal × 0.8716 = 98 × 0.8716 = 85.42 inches
Height = Diagonal × 0.4903 = 98 × 0.4903 = 48.05 inches
workedExamples.wrongApproach: Simply dividing the diagonal by 2 to get width and height is incorrect. The diagonal, width, and height form a right triangle — you must use the aspect ratio multipliers or the Pythagorean theorem.

workedExamples.given: A conference room with the farthest viewer at 24 feet from the screen. Content is standard business presentations (BADM).
workedExamples.asked: What is the minimum display diagonal for a 16:9 display?
workedExamples.solution:
BADM = 6H maximum viewing distance
Minimum image height = 24 feet / 6 = 4 feet = 48 inches
Diagonal = Height / 0.4903 = 48 / 0.4903 = 97.9 inches
workedExamples.answer: Minimum 98-inch diagonal display (round up to next available size)
workedExamples.wrongApproach: Using BDM (8H) instead of BADM (6H) would give: 24/8 = 3 feet = 36 inches height → 73.4-inch diagonal. This undersizes the display — viewers in the back row cannot read presentation text.

workedExamples.given: A projector with a 1.5:1 to 2.0:1 zoom lens range needs to produce a 150-inch wide image.
workedExamples.asked: What are the minimum and maximum throw distances this projector can be mounted at?
workedExamples.solution:
Minimum throw distance = 1.5 × 150 = 225 inches = 18.75 feet
Maximum throw distance = 2.0 × 150 = 300 inches = 25.0 feet
workedExamples.answer: The projector can be mounted between 18.75 feet and 25 feet from the screen.
workedExamples.wrongApproach: Dividing image width by throw ratio instead of multiplying gives the inverse (100 inches and 75 inches) — completely wrong distances that would produce an undersized image.

lessons.examRelevance: Display sizing using DISCAS and throw ratio calculations are among the most commonly tested math topics on the CTS exam. Know the content categories (BDM=8H, BADM=6H, ADM=4H) and how to calculate both minimum display size from viewing distance and projector throw distance. The formulas are provided — focus on selecting the right formula and values.

knowledgeCheck.question: For Analytical Decision Making (ADM) content like spreadsheets, what is the maximum viewing distance according to DISCAS?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: ADM content (spreadsheets, detailed data) requires a maximum viewing distance of 4H. The more detailed the content, the closer viewers must be (or the larger the display must be).

knowledgeCheck.question: A projector has a throw ratio of 2.0:1. To produce a 100-inch wide image, what throw distance is required?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Throw Distance = Throw Ratio × Image Width = 2.0 × 100 = 200 inches. The throw ratio tells you how many image-widths away the projector must be from the screen.

memorize: 16:9 multipliers: Width = Diag × 0.872, Height = Diag × 0.490
DISCAS: BDM=8H, BADM=6H, ADM=4H, Forensic=2H
Throw Ratio = Throw Distance / Image Width
Standard business content = BADM (6H)
understand: Higher screen gain means brighter center but narrower viewing angle — not always better
DISCAS content categories match content detail level to viewing distance
Throw ratio is inversely related to image size at a fixed distance
practice: Calculate display size for rooms with different farthest viewer distances
Convert between diagonal, width, and height for 16:9 and 4:3 displays
Determine projector throw distances for different lens options
examTraps: Don't use BDM (8H) for spreadsheet content — spreadsheets are ADM (4H)
Throw ratio uses IMAGE WIDTH, not diagonal
When calculating minimum display size, always use the FARTHEST viewer, not the closest
studyNotes.fieldTip: In practice, always round UP to the next available display size. If your calculation says you need 97.9 inches, specify a 98-inch display. Undersizing creates complaints; slight oversizing is never a problem.

lessons.summary: Display sizing relies on DISCAS content categories (BDM=8H, BADM=6H, ADM=4H, Forensic=2H) to determine minimum image height from farthest viewer distance. For 16:9 displays, Width = Diagonal × 0.872 and Height = Diagonal × 0.490. Projector throw ratio = Distance / Width. Higher screen gain increases brightness but narrows viewing angle. Always size displays based on the most detailed content type and the farthest viewer.

lessons.title: AV Math: Electrical, Power, Decibels & Sound
lessons.module: Day 1: CTS Foundations, Standards & AV Math
lessons.overview: Master the electrical and acoustical math essential for AV system design: Ohm's Law, power calculations, circuit sizing, BTU heat loads, the decibel scale for both power and voltage, the inverse square law, SPL measurements, and noise criteria ratings.
learningObjectives: Apply Ohm's Law and power formulas to AV circuit calculations
Calculate circuit breaker sizing using the 80% continuous load rule
Use decibel formulas for power ratios and voltage/distance ratios
Apply the inverse square law to predict sound level changes with distance
Interpret SPL measurements and Noise Criteria (NC) ratings for room acoustics

keyTerms.definition: The fundamental electrical relationship: Voltage (V) = Current (I) × Resistance (R). Also expressed as I = V/R and R = V/I. The foundation of all electrical calculations.
The unit of electrical power. Power = Voltage × Current (P = V × I). Also calculated as P = I²R or P = V²/R.

A logarithmic unit expressing the ratio between two values. For power: dB = 10 × log₁₀(P₁/P₂). For voltage or distance: dB = 20 × log₁₀(V₁/V₂). Used extensively in audio for SPL, gain, and signal levels.

Sound intensity decreases by 6 dB each time the distance from the source doubles. This applies to point sources in free field conditions. At 2× distance, SPL drops 6 dB; at 4× distance, SPL drops 12 dB.
The measurement of sound intensity in decibels, referenced to the threshold of human hearing (0 dB SPL = 20 micropascals). Normal conversation is approximately 60 dB SPL.

A rating system for background noise levels in rooms. Lower NC values mean quieter rooms. Typical targets: NC-25 for recording studios, NC-30 for conference rooms, NC-35 for open offices, NC-40 for lobbies.
NEC requirement that continuous loads (running 3+ hours) may not exceed 80% of the circuit breaker rating. A 20-amp circuit supports a maximum continuous load of 16 amps (20 × 0.80).
The unit of electrical current flow. Current = Power / Voltage (I = P/V). Critical for determining circuit and breaker requirements.
British Thermal Units per hour. The heat output measure used by HVAC engineers. Convert from watts: BTU/hr = Watts × 3.412.

lessons.content:
OHM'S LAW — THE FOUNDATION

Ohm's Law describes the relationship between voltage, current, and resistance in an electrical circuit:

V = I × R

Where:
- V = Voltage in volts (the electrical pressure pushing current through a circuit)
- I = Current in amperes/amps (the flow of electrons through a circuit)
- R = Resistance in ohms (the opposition to current flow)

Rearranged:
- I = V / R (to find current)
- R = V / I (to find resistance)

In AV, Ohm's Law is used for speaker impedance calculations, cable resistance, and basic circuit analysis.

POWER FORMULAS

Electrical power is measured in watts (W):

P = V × I (Power = Voltage × Current)

Alternate forms:
- P = I² × R (Power from current and resistance)
- P = V² / R (Power from voltage and resistance)

These formulas are essential for:
- Determining how much current AV equipment draws
- Sizing circuits and breakers
- Calculating heat loads for HVAC

CIRCUIT SIZING AND THE 80% RULE

The NEC requires that continuous loads (operating for 3 hours or more — which includes most AV equipment) not exceed 80% of the circuit breaker rating.

80% Rule: Maximum continuous load = Breaker rating × 0.80

Common circuit sizes:
- 15-amp circuit at 120V: Max continuous load = 15 × 0.80 = 12 amps = 1,440 watts
- 20-amp circuit at 120V: Max continuous load = 20 × 0.80 = 16 amps = 1,920 watts
- 20-amp circuit at 208V: Max continuous load = 20 × 0.80 = 16 amps = 3,328 watts

To determine how many circuits you need:
1. Sum all AV equipment wattage
2. Divide by voltage to get total amps
3. Apply the 80% rule: divide total amps by 0.80 to get minimum breaker rating
4. Select the next standard breaker size up

THE DECIBEL SCALE

Decibels (dB) express ratios on a logarithmic scale. This is critical because human hearing perceives sound logarithmically, and audio signals span enormous ranges.

Two formulas — which one to use depends on what you are comparing:

For POWER ratios: dB = 10 × log₁₀(P₁/P₂)
For VOLTAGE, SOUND PRESSURE, or DISTANCE ratios: dB = 20 × log₁₀(V₁/V₂)

Key dB relationships to memorize:
- Doubling power = +3 dB (10 × log₁₀(2) = 3.01)
- Halving power = -3 dB
- 10× power = +10 dB
- 100× power = +20 dB
- Doubling voltage or SPL = +6 dB (20 × log₁₀(2) = 6.02)
- Halving voltage or SPL = -6 dB

Practical audio reference: Perceived loudness roughly doubles with every +10 dB increase. A 70 dB sound seems about twice as loud as a 60 dB sound.

THE INVERSE SQUARE LAW

The inverse square law governs how sound level decreases with distance from a point source in free field (no reflections):

Every doubling of distance = -6 dB SPL

Formula: dB change = 20 × log₁₀(D₁/D₂)

Where D₁ is the original distance and D₂ is the new distance.

Examples:
- Speaker produces 90 dB SPL at 1 meter
- At 2 meters: 90 - 6 = 84 dB SPL
- At 4 meters: 90 - 12 = 78 dB SPL
- At 8 meters: 90 - 18 = 72 dB SPL
- At 16 meters: 90 - 24 = 66 dB SPL

Note: The inverse square law applies to point sources in free field. Indoors, reflections from walls, ceiling, and floor modify this — actual SPL drop is typically less than 6 dB per doubling due to reflected sound energy.

Line arrays and column speakers are designed to defeat the inverse square law — they produce cylindrical wavefronts that drop only 3 dB per doubling of distance, extending coverage much farther.

SOUND PRESSURE LEVEL (SPL) REFERENCES

Common SPL values:
- 0 dB SPL: Threshold of human hearing
- 30 dB: Quiet room, whisper
- 50 dB: Quiet office
- 60 dB: Normal conversation at 3 feet
- 70 dB: Typical speech reinforcement target
- 85 dB: Maximum prolonged exposure without hearing protection (OSHA)
- 100 dB: Front row of a rock concert
- 120 dB: Threshold of pain
- 140 dB: Jet engine at close range

For speech reinforcement, the target SPL is typically 65-75 dB at the farthest listener. The system must produce this level above the background noise — a minimum signal-to-noise ratio of 15-25 dB is recommended for good speech intelligibility.

NOISE CRITERIA (NC) RATINGS

NC ratings quantify the acceptable background noise level in a room. They are measured with all building systems running (HVAC, lighting, etc.) but no AV system active.

Common NC targets:
- NC-15 to NC-20: Recording studios, concert halls
- NC-25: Worship spaces, theaters, courtrooms
- NC-30: Executive conference rooms, teleconference rooms
- NC-35: Standard conference rooms, classrooms
- NC-40: Open office, lobbies
- NC-45: Workshops, kitchens

Lower NC = quieter room = less background noise = easier to achieve good speech intelligibility.

Why NC matters for AV design: If the room's NC rating is too high, even a well-designed audio system will struggle with intelligibility. The signal (speech) must be sufficiently louder than the noise (background). NC ratings help you determine whether acoustic treatment or HVAC modifications are needed before installing audio equipment.

HEAT LOAD CALCULATIONS

All electrical power consumed by AV equipment is eventually converted to heat:

BTU/hr = Watts × 3.412

This calculation must be provided to the HVAC engineer for every equipment room, rack closet, and projection booth. Inadequate cooling is one of the top causes of AV equipment failure.

scenarios.situation: You are designing an AV system for a conference room with equipment totaling 2,200 watts on a single 120V circuit.
scenarios.notice: At 120V, 2,200 watts draws 18.3 amps (2,200/120). A 20-amp circuit at 80% continuous load is limited to 16 amps (1,920 watts). The equipment exceeds the circuit capacity.
scenarios.nextStep: Either split the load across two 20-amp circuits or request a single 30-amp circuit (30 × 0.80 = 24 amps = 2,880 watts capacity at 120V).
scenarios.whyMatters: Overloading circuits trips breakers during events, causing system failures. Circuit sizing with the 80% rule is tested on the CTS exam and is a real-world safety requirement.

scenarios.situation: A speaker produces 90 dB SPL at 1 meter, and you need to know the SPL at the farthest seat, which is 16 meters away.
scenarios.notice: 16 meters is 4 doublings of distance from 1 meter (1→2→4→8→16). Each doubling drops SPL by 6 dB.
scenarios.nextStep: SPL at 16m = 90 - (4 × 6) = 90 - 24 = 66 dB SPL. If the background noise is NC-35 (approximately 35-40 dB), the signal-to-noise ratio is about 26-31 dB — acceptable for speech.
scenarios.whyMatters: The inverse square law determines whether a speaker can provide adequate coverage at the farthest listening position. This calculation drives speaker selection and quantity.

workedExamples.given: An AV rack contains equipment totaling 3,000 watts, powered by 120V circuits.
workedExamples.solution:
Total current = P/V = 3,000/120 = 25 amps
80% rule: each 20A circuit supports 20 × 0.80 = 16 amps continuous
Circuits needed = 25/16 = 1.5625
Round up to 2 circuits (you cannot install half a circuit)
workedExamples.wrongApproach: Dividing 3,000W by 20A (= 150) makes no sense dimensionally. Or using the full 20A without the 80% rule would say 25/20 = 1.25 → 2 circuits — same answer here, but this approach is wrong because it violates the 80% continuous load rule.

workedExamples.given: An amplifier outputs 100 watts. You upgrade to an amplifier that outputs 200 watts.
workedExamples.asked: How many decibels louder is the 200-watt amplifier?
workedExamples.wrongApproach: Using the voltage formula (20 × log) instead of the power formula (10 × log) would give 6 dB — wrong. Remember: 10× log for power, 20× log for voltage/SPL/distance.

workedExamples.given: A speaker produces 94 dB SPL at 1 meter.
workedExamples.asked: What is the SPL at 8 meters?
workedExamples.solution:
8 meters = 3 doublings of distance (1→2→4→8)
Each doubling = -6 dB
Total drop = 3 × 6 = 18 dB
SPL at 8m = 94 - 18 = 76 dB SPL
workedExamples.wrongApproach: Using -3 dB per doubling (that is for power, not distance) would give 94 - 9 = 85 dB — significantly overestimating the actual SPL at distance.

workedExamples.given: An AV rack draws 2,500 watts total.
workedExamples.asked: Calculate the heat load in BTU/hr.
workedExamples.wrongApproach: Dividing by 3.412 instead of multiplying gives 732 BTU/hr — a massive underestimate that would result in inadequate cooling.

lessons.examRelevance: Electrical and decibel calculations are among the most frequently tested math topics. The CTS exam provides formulas, but you must know: Ohm's Law (V=IR), Power (P=VI), 80% circuit rule, dB for power (10×log) vs. dB for voltage/distance (20×log), inverse square law (-6 dB per doubling), and BTU conversion (W × 3.412). Expect 5-8 questions involving these calculations.

knowledgeCheck.question: According to the NEC 80% rule, what is the maximum continuous load on a 20-amp, 120V circuit?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: 80% of 20 amps = 16 amps continuous. Power = V × I = 120V × 16A = 1,920 watts. This is the NEC maximum for continuous loads on a 20-amp circuit.

knowledgeCheck.question: By how many decibels does sound decrease when you double the distance from a point source?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The inverse square law states that SPL decreases by 6 dB for every doubling of distance from a point source in free field. This uses the 20×log formula: 20 × log(1/2) = -6.02 dB.

memorize: V = IR, P = VI
80% rule: max continuous = breaker × 0.80
Power dB: 10 × log(ratio), Voltage/Distance dB: 20 × log(ratio)
Double power = +3 dB, Double voltage = +6 dB
Inverse square law: -6 dB per doubling of distance
BTU/hr = Watts × 3.412
NC-30 for conference rooms, NC-25 for critical listening
understand: The 10×log vs 20×log distinction — power uses 10, voltage/pressure/distance uses 20
Inverse square law applies to point sources in free field — indoors, actual drop is less due to reflections
NC ratings measure background noise WITHOUT the AV system active
practice: Calculate circuit requirements for different equipment loads
Predict SPL at various distances using the inverse square law
Convert between watts and BTU/hr
examTraps: 10×log for POWER, 20×log for VOLTAGE/SPL — using the wrong formula doubles or halves your answer
Inverse square law is -6 dB per doubling, not -3 dB — do not confuse with power doubling
The 80% rule applies to CONTINUOUS loads (3+ hours) — intermittent loads can use the full circuit rating
studyNotes.fieldTip: Always request dedicated AV circuits, not shared circuits with other building systems. A vacuum cleaner or coffee maker on a shared circuit can trip the breaker during a presentation.

lessons.summary: Essential AV electrical math: Ohm's Law (V=IR), Power (P=VI), circuit sizing with the 80% rule (20A × 0.80 = 16A max continuous), decibels for power (10×log) and voltage/distance (20×log), inverse square law (-6 dB per doubling of distance), NC ratings for background noise, and BTU/hr = Watts × 3.412 for heat loads. Double power = +3 dB; double distance = -6 dB.

lessons.title: Needs Analysis & Stakeholder Discovery
lessons.module: Day 1: CTS Foundations, Standards & AV Math
lessons.overview: Learn the systematic process for identifying stakeholders, gathering functional requirements, translating client needs into AV system specifications, and documenting the program report that drives all subsequent design decisions.
learningObjectives: Identify all stakeholder types and their roles in an AV project's decision-making process
Distinguish between functional requirements and technical specifications
Conduct effective stakeholder interviews using structured discovery questions
Translate non-technical client language into actionable AV system requirements
Create a program report that captures scope, requirements, and constraints

keyTerms.definition: A statement describing what the AV system must DO from the user's perspective, independent of specific technology. Example: 'Remote participants must see and hear all in-room presenters clearly.'

A statement describing HOW the system will meet a functional requirement using specific technology. Example: 'Install a PTZ camera with 20× optical zoom and a ceiling microphone array.' Specifications come AFTER requirements, not before.
Any individual or group with a vested interest in the AV project outcome. Categories include decision makers, end users, technical support staff, and allied professionals.

The formal document produced at the end of needs analysis that captures all functional requirements, site conditions, constraints, assumptions, and design intent. It is the foundation for all design work.
A structured statement of need: 'As a [role], I need to [action], so that [benefit].' User stories focus on outcomes rather than technology solutions.
The process of comparing a client's needs and expectations against similar existing installations to establish realistic performance expectations, budget ranges, and technology recommendations.
The uncontrolled expansion of project requirements beyond the original scope, typically caused by undocumented assumptions, unclear requirements, or stakeholder additions after design begins.

Meeting the accessibility requirements of the Americans with Disabilities Act, including assistive listening systems in assembly areas, accessible control panel heights, visual notification, and captioning capabilities.

lessons.content:
THE NEEDS ANALYSIS PROCESS

Needs analysis is the first and most critical phase of any AV project. It answers the fundamental question: what does this system need to do? Every design decision that follows — equipment selection, system architecture, installation approach, budget — flows from the requirements established during needs analysis.

The process follows a structured sequence:
1. Identify stakeholders
2. Conduct stakeholder interviews and discovery sessions
3. Perform site survey (covered in Lesson 8)
4. Document functional requirements
5. Establish constraints (budget, schedule, infrastructure, aesthetics)
6. Create the program report

IDENTIFYING STAKEHOLDERS

Missing a key stakeholder is one of the most common — and costly — AV project mistakes. Every stakeholder group has different needs and priorities:

Executive Sponsors / Decision Makers: They control budget and approval. They care about business outcomes, ROI, and organizational image. They may not understand technology but know what they want the system to achieve for the organization.

End Users / Operators: The people who use the system daily. They care about ease of use, reliability, and whether the system helps them do their job. Their input is critical for user interface design and system complexity decisions.

IT Department: They manage the network, security policies, and often ongoing AV support. Their requirements around VLANs, bandwidth, security protocols, and remote management directly impact system design. Failing to involve IT early is a recipe for network conflicts during installation.

Facilities / Maintenance Staff: They maintain the building, manage HVAC, control access to equipment rooms, and often handle first-line AV troubleshooting. Their input affects equipment placement, accessibility for maintenance, and labeling requirements.

Architects / Interior Designers: They control the aesthetics of the space. AV equipment must integrate with their design intent. Display sizes, speaker grilles, control panel finishes, and cable pathway concealment must be coordinated with architectural design.

Acousticians: In critical listening spaces, acoustic consultants specify room treatment, noise isolation, and HVAC noise targets that directly affect AV audio system design.

Security: In government, military, and some corporate environments, security stakeholders dictate equipment restrictions, network isolation requirements, and physical access controls.

CONDUCTING EFFECTIVE DISCOVERY

Structured discovery questions extract functional requirements without leading the client toward specific technology:

Communication Questions:
- Who needs to communicate with whom? (one-to-many, many-to-many, point-to-point)
- Are remote participants involved? How often? How many?
- What is the primary mode of communication? (presentation, discussion, collaboration)

Content Questions:
- What types of content will be shared? (slides, video, spreadsheets, whiteboards, documents)
- How many simultaneous sources need to be visible?
- Is content archiving or recording required?

User Experience Questions:
- What is the technical skill level of the typical operator?
- Is a dedicated AV operator available, or must the system be self-service?
- How quickly must the system be ready for use? (walk-in-and-present vs. scheduled startup)

Environment Questions:
- What are the lighting conditions? Can lights be dimmed or controlled?
- What is the ambient noise level? Are there noise sources that cannot be eliminated?
- How many occupants at maximum capacity?

Constraint Questions:
- What is the budget range?
- When must the system be operational?
- Are there aesthetic restrictions from the architect or designer?
- Are there network or security policies that restrict equipment choices?

TRANSLATING CLIENT LANGUAGE

Clients describe needs in their language, not AV language. Your job is to translate:

Client says: 'We need better audio in here — people on the phone can't hear us.'
Translation: The room needs acoustic echo cancellation, a ceiling microphone array or boundary mics for full coverage, and potentially acoustic treatment to reduce reverberation.

Client says: 'We want the room to be simple — just walk in and go.'
Translation: The control system needs occupancy sensing or a single-button start. Source auto-detection for BYOD. No complex menus or manual switching.

Client says: 'We do a lot of Zoom calls.'
Translation: The room needs a UC-certified system with camera, microphones, speakers, and display. Confirm platform (Zoom Rooms, Teams Rooms, BYOD, or multi-platform). Design for the camera's field of view to cover all seating positions.

THE PROGRAM REPORT

The program report is the deliverable of the needs analysis phase. It documents:

1. Project overview and objectives
2. Stakeholder list and their roles
3. Functional requirements (organized by room or space)
4. Site conditions and constraints
5. Assumptions and exclusions
6. Budget range and phasing (if applicable)
7. Schedule requirements and milestones
8. Accessibility requirements (ADA)
9. Technology preferences and restrictions
10. Approval signatures

The program report is a contract between the AV team and the client. Any requirements not in the program report are scope creep. Any requirements IN the program report must be addressed in the design.

ADA AND ACCESSIBILITY REQUIREMENTS

For AV projects, ADA compliance includes:
- Assistive listening systems in assembly areas with audio amplification (required by law)
- Touch panel controls mounted between 15-48 inches AFF for wheelchair accessibility
- Visual notification devices (strobes) in addition to audible signals
- Captioning capability for public-facing video content
- Accessible routes to AV operator positions
- Hearing loop or IR assistive listening receivers available at a minimum ratio (typically 4% of seating capacity, with 25% of those being hearing-aid compatible)

scenarios.situation: During a stakeholder meeting for a new corporate boardroom, the CEO describes the system they want by naming specific products they saw at a competitor's facility.
scenarios.notice: The CEO is specifying solutions rather than requirements. Their competitor's system may not be appropriate for this room's size, use case, or IT infrastructure.
scenarios.nextStep: Acknowledge their reference point, then redirect to functional discovery: 'That's helpful context. Let me understand how your team will use this room day-to-day so we can design the best solution for your specific needs.' Document the competitor reference as a benchmark, not as a requirement.
scenarios.whyMatters: The CTS exam tests the difference between functional requirements and technical specifications. A skilled AV professional translates client product requests into functional needs, then recommends the appropriate technology.

scenarios.situation: The AV design is nearly complete when the IT director — who was not included in the original stakeholder meetings — raises concerns about multicast traffic on the corporate network.
scenarios.notice: A critical stakeholder was missed during discovery. IT's network policies directly impact the AV system design, particularly for AV-over-IP and control system networking.
scenarios.nextStep: Immediately schedule a coordination meeting with IT. Document their network requirements and assess the impact on the current design. This may require design changes and potentially a change order if the scope is affected.
scenarios.whyMatters: Missing stakeholders cause late-stage redesigns, budget overruns, and project delays. The CTS exam emphasizes identifying ALL stakeholders during the needs analysis phase, not after design begins.

lessons.examRelevance: Needs analysis falls squarely in Domain 1 (Creating AV Solutions — 35%). Expect questions that test your ability to distinguish functional requirements from technical specifications, identify the correct stakeholder for a given decision, and determine the proper next step in the discovery process. Scenario-based questions often present a client statement and ask you to identify the underlying functional requirement.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which of the following is a functional requirement?
options: Install a 75-inch Samsung display on the east wall
Use Crestron control with a 10-inch touch panel
All participants must clearly see shared content from any seat in the room
Run two Cat6A cables to each display location
knowledgeCheck.answer: All participants must clearly see shared content from any seat in the room
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A functional requirement describes what the system must achieve from the user's perspective without specifying technology. 'All participants must clearly see shared content from any seat' describes the need — the display type, size, and mounting are the technical specifications that fulfill it.

knowledgeCheck.question: When during the AV project lifecycle should stakeholder identification occur?
options: During the needs analysis / program phase
knowledgeCheck.answer: During the needs analysis / program phase
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Stakeholder identification is a foundational step in needs analysis — the very first phase of an AV project. Discovering stakeholders later causes design revisions, scope creep, and delays.

memorize: Stakeholder categories: Decision makers, End users, IT, Facilities, Architects, Acousticians, Security
Program report = the deliverable of needs analysis
ADA: assistive listening required in assembly areas with audio amplification
ADA control height: 15-48 inches AFF
understand: Functional requirements describe WHAT, technical specifications describe HOW
User stories format: As a [role], I need to [action], so that [benefit]
Missing stakeholders is one of the most costly project mistakes — it causes late redesigns
practice: Convert client product requests into functional requirements
Write user stories for common AV scenarios (conference room, lecture hall, lobby display)
examTraps: The person requesting the system is often NOT the primary end user — design for actual users
A client naming a specific product is NOT stating a functional requirement
Scope creep starts when requirements are undocumented — the program report prevents this
studyNotes.fieldTip: Always interview end users separately from decision makers. Users are more honest about their actual needs when the boss isn't in the room. A CEO may want impressive technology; the users want something that works reliably every time.

lessons.summary: Needs analysis identifies stakeholders (decision makers, end users, IT, facilities, architects), gathers functional requirements through structured discovery, and documents everything in a program report. Functional requirements describe WHAT the system must do; technical specifications describe HOW. Missing stakeholders cause costly redesigns. The program report is the foundation document that prevents scope creep and drives all design decisions.

lessons.title: Site Survey: Process, Tools, Conditions & Documentation
lessons.module: Day 1: CTS Foundations, Standards & AV Math
lessons.overview: Master the site survey process including pre-design and pre-installation surveys, measurement tools and techniques, documenting environmental conditions, assessing existing infrastructure, and creating the survey report that informs AV system design.
learningObjectives: Differentiate between pre-design and pre-installation site surveys
Identify the tools and instruments used for AV site surveys
Document room dimensions, ambient light, ambient noise, and existing infrastructure
Assess structural conditions that affect equipment mounting and cable routing
Produce a comprehensive site survey report with measurements and photographs

keyTerms.definition: A site survey conducted before system design begins, focused on gathering environmental data, dimensions, infrastructure conditions, and constraints that will inform the AV design. Also called a design survey or initial survey.
A site survey conducted after design is complete but before installation begins, to verify that actual site conditions match the design assumptions and that the space is ready for AV installation.

The existing light in a space from all sources including windows, skylights, and artificial lighting. Measured in lux (metric) or foot-candles (US). High ambient light affects display contrast and projector performance.

Background sound in a space from HVAC systems, adjacent rooms, exterior sources, and building systems. Measured in dB SPL or characterized by NC rating. Affects audio system design and speech intelligibility.
US unit of illuminance. 1 foot-candle = 1 lumen per square foot. Measured with a light meter. Typical office lighting is 30-50 fc. Conversion: 1 fc = 10.764 lux.
SI/metric unit of illuminance. 1 lux = 1 lumen per square meter. Typical office: 300-500 lux. Outdoor daylight: 10,000-100,000 lux.

The construction of the ceiling, which affects speaker mounting, cable routing, and projector installation. Types include suspended/drop ceiling (accessible), drywall/gypsum (requires backing or structural support), exposed structure (open ceiling), and concrete (limited mounting options).
Tubing or pipe used to protect and route cables through walls, ceilings, and floors. AV surveyors must identify existing conduit paths and assess capacity for new cable runs.

lessons.content:
THE PURPOSE OF A SITE SURVEY

A site survey is the physical inspection of a project location to gather the real-world data that drives AV system design. No matter how good the architectural drawings are, nothing replaces eyes-on-site measurement and documentation. Site conditions frequently differ from drawings — walls are not where plans show them, ceiling heights vary, infrastructure does not exist where expected, and environmental conditions cannot be assessed from a floor plan.

There are two types of site surveys, conducted at different project phases:

PRE-DESIGN SURVEY

Conducted during or immediately after needs analysis, before design begins. The pre-design survey establishes the physical reality of the space:

Room Dimensions:
- Length, width, and ceiling height (measure at multiple points — ceilings are often not level)
- Irregularities: alcoves, columns, soffits, angled walls, stepped floors
- Door locations and swing directions (affects equipment placement and sight lines)
- Window locations, sizes, and orientation (north, south, east, west affects sunlight)

Ambient Light Assessment:
- Measure light levels at the planned screen/display location using a light meter
- Measure with all room lights on and window coverings open (worst case)
- Measure with lights dimmed and coverings closed (best case)
- Note controllability: are there dimmable lights? Motorized shades? Blackout capability?
- Light level directly impacts display technology choice — high ambient light favors direct-view displays over projection

Ambient Noise Assessment:
- Measure background noise with an SPL meter at the listener positions
- HVAC must be running during measurement — it is the primary noise source
- Note intermittent noise sources: elevator shafts, mechanical rooms, adjacent ballrooms, exterior traffic
- High background noise requires more powerful audio systems and may necessitate acoustic treatment

Existing Infrastructure:
- Electrical: number of circuits, locations of outlets, panel locations, available capacity
- Network: data drops, switch locations, available ports, VLAN configuration
- Cable pathways: existing conduit, cable trays, J-hooks, accessible pathways
- HVAC: duct locations, register positions (these cause noise near microphones)
- Structural: wall construction (drywall, concrete, glass), ceiling type, floor type

Sight Lines:
- From every seating position, can viewers see the planned display location without obstruction?
- Are there columns, soffits, or furniture that block views?
- What is the viewing angle from extreme side seats? (Maximum recommended: 45° from screen center)
- What is the vertical viewing angle? (Bottom of display should be at standing presenter's eye level or higher)

PRE-INSTALLATION SURVEY

Conducted after design is complete, typically 2-4 weeks before installation begins. This survey verifies:
- Room dimensions match design drawings
- Specified cable pathways exist and have capacity
- Electrical circuits are installed and energized
- Network drops are in place
- Structural backing is installed for display/projector/speaker mounting
- Other trades (electrical, HVAC, ceiling) are complete or on schedule
- The space is accessible for equipment delivery (elevators, doorways, loading docks)

SITE SURVEY TOOLS

Essential tools for an AV site survey:

- Laser Distance Measure: Accurate room dimensions (±1/16 inch). Essential for measuring room length, width, height, and distances between features.
- Light Meter (Lux Meter): Measures ambient illumination in lux or foot-candles. Critical for display/projection decisions.
- SPL Meter: Measures ambient noise levels in decibels. Used with HVAC running to assess background noise conditions.
- Tape Measure: For quick measurements, equipment dimensions, and cable run estimates.
- Digital Camera/Phone: Photograph everything — walls, ceilings, cable pathways, existing equipment, electrical panels, potential obstructions. Photos are invaluable during design.
- Stud Finder: Locates structural framing behind drywall for mounting points.
- Scale Rule: For referencing architectural drawings on-site.
- Flashlight: For inspecting above-ceiling spaces, behind racks, and in equipment closets.
- Network Cable Tester: Verifies existing data cable continuity and identifies cable types.
- Outlet Tester: Verifies electrical outlets are properly wired and grounded.

DOCUMENTATION AND REPORTING

The site survey report should include:
1. Room name, location, and building information
2. All dimensions with measurement method noted
3. Ambient light readings with conditions (lights on/off, shades open/closed)
4. Ambient noise readings with HVAC state noted
5. Existing infrastructure inventory (power, data, cable pathways)
6. Ceiling type and height
7. Wall construction and condition
8. Furniture layout (current and planned)
9. Photographs keyed to a floor plan
10. Identified constraints or concerns
11. Discrepancies between drawings and actual conditions
12. Recommendations for pre-installation work by other trades

COMMON SITE SURVEY MISTAKES

- Measuring room dimensions with HVAC off — you need noise readings with HVAC running
- Taking light readings at only one time of day — afternoon sun through west-facing windows creates problems not visible in the morning
- Not checking above the ceiling — critical for cable routing, structural conditions, and fire stops
- Assuming architectural drawings are accurate — always verify with on-site measurements
- Forgetting to document furniture layout — furniture affects sight lines, speaker placement, and microphone coverage

scenarios.situation: During a pre-design survey, you measure the ambient light at the proposed screen location and get a reading of 500 lux (46 foot-candles) with window shades open.
scenarios.notice: 500 lux is high ambient light. A standard projector will struggle to produce adequate contrast against this lighting. Even a bright projector (5,000+ lumens) will appear washed out.
scenarios.nextStep: Document the light level and controllability options. Recommend either a direct-view display (LCD/LED panel which performs well in high ambient light), motorized blackout shades for the windows, or an ALR (ambient light rejecting) projection screen if projection is required.
scenarios.whyMatters: Ambient light measurement directly drives the display technology decision. The CTS exam tests your ability to select the appropriate display technology based on environmental conditions.

scenarios.situation: The pre-installation survey reveals that the structural backing specified for a 98-inch display has not been installed behind the drywall.
scenarios.notice: Without structural backing, the display cannot be safely mounted. Standard drywall cannot support the weight of a large commercial display (typically 80-150 pounds).
scenarios.nextStep: Document the discrepancy, notify the general contractor and project manager immediately. The backing must be installed before drywall finishing in that area. This may require a schedule adjustment.
scenarios.whyMatters: Pre-installation surveys exist specifically to catch issues like this before the AV crew arrives. Discovering missing backing on installation day causes costly delays and schedule disruption.

lessons.examRelevance: Site survey questions appear in Domain 1 (Creating AV Solutions). The CTS exam tests your knowledge of what to measure and document during a survey, which tools to use, and how survey data influences design decisions. Expect questions about ambient light's impact on display selection and ambient noise's impact on audio design.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the primary difference between a pre-design survey and a pre-installation survey?
options: Pre-design uses more tools than pre-installation
Pre-design gathers data for design; pre-installation verifies the space is ready for installation
Pre-design is conducted by the consultant; pre-installation by the installer
Pre-design is optional; pre-installation is required
knowledgeCheck.answer: Pre-design gathers data for design; pre-installation verifies the space is ready for installation
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Pre-design surveys collect environmental data and site conditions that inform the AV system design. Pre-installation surveys verify that actual conditions match design assumptions and that prerequisite work by other trades is complete.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which tool would you use to measure background noise levels during a site survey?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: An SPL (Sound Pressure Level) meter measures sound levels in decibels. During a site survey, it is used with HVAC systems running to measure background noise, which affects audio system design and speech intelligibility requirements.

memorize: Pre-design survey: before design, gathers data. Pre-install survey: before installation, verifies readiness.
Light meter measures lux or foot-candles. SPL meter measures decibels.
1 foot-candle = 10.764 lux
Maximum viewing angle from screen center: 45°
Typical office lighting: 30-50 fc (300-500 lux)
understand: Ambient light drives display technology choice (high light = direct-view display preferred over projection)
Ambient noise affects audio design — higher noise requires more powerful systems or acoustic treatment
Site conditions frequently differ from architectural drawings — always verify on-site
practice: List the 10 items you would document in a site survey report
Identify which survey tool addresses each type of measurement
examTraps: HVAC must be running during noise measurements — measurements with HVAC off are meaningless for design
Light readings vary by time of day — afternoon sun through windows creates different conditions than morning
A pre-installation survey is NOT a substitute for a pre-design survey — they serve different purposes
studyNotes.fieldTip: Always take more photos than you think you need during a site survey. You cannot photograph the space once drywall is up and ceilings are closed. Above-ceiling photos showing structural conditions, existing cable pathways, and fire stops save repeated site visits.

lessons.summary: Site surveys gather the physical reality that drives AV design. Pre-design surveys collect dimensions, ambient light (lux meter), ambient noise (SPL meter), existing infrastructure, and sight lines before design begins. Pre-installation surveys verify readiness for installation. Key tools include laser distance measures, light meters, SPL meters, and cameras. High ambient light favors direct-view displays; high ambient noise requires more powerful audio or acoustic treatment. Always verify site conditions — never rely solely on architectural drawings.

lessons.title: Audio Fundamentals: Signal Flow, Mics & Speakers
lessons.module: Day 2: Audio, Video, Control Systems & Networking
lessons.domainAlignment: Domain 1: Creating AV Solutions (35%) / Domain 2: Operating AV Solutions (20%)
lessons.overview: Understand the complete audio signal chain from microphone to speaker, including signal types, connectors, microphone technologies and polar patterns, speaker types and coverage, balanced versus unbalanced wiring, and phantom power.
learningObjectives: Trace the complete audio signal flow from source through processing to output
Distinguish between mic level, line level, and speaker level signals
Compare balanced and unbalanced audio connections and explain why balanced is preferred
Identify microphone types and their appropriate applications based on polar pattern
Select appropriate speaker types based on coverage requirements and room characteristics

keyTerms.definition: The path an audio signal travels from source (microphone, media player) through processing (mixer, DSP) and amplification to output (speakers). Understanding signal flow is essential for system design and troubleshooting.
The weakest audio signal level, output by microphones. Typically -60 dBV to -40 dBV. Requires preamplification to reach line level. Very susceptible to interference without balanced wiring.
The standard signal level for audio processing equipment. Professional line level is +4 dBu; consumer line level is -10 dBV. Most audio processing (mixing, DSP, routing) operates at line level.
The amplified signal level sent from a power amplifier to speakers. Much higher voltage and current than mic or line level. Carried on speaker wire, not shielded audio cable.

A wiring method using three conductors (positive, negative, ground) to reject electromagnetic interference. The positive and negative signals are equal but opposite in polarity; when combined at the receiving device, noise picked up along the cable is cancelled. Uses XLR or TRS connectors.
A wiring method using two conductors (signal, ground). Susceptible to electromagnetic interference, especially over long cable runs. Uses RCA or TS connectors. Maximum recommended run: 15-25 feet.
The standard professional audio connector for balanced mic and line level signals. 3-pin XLR is most common: Pin 1 = Ground, Pin 2 = Hot (+), Pin 3 = Cold (-). Also carries phantom power.
Tip-Ring-Sleeve connector (1/4 inch or 3.5mm) used for balanced mono connections or unbalanced stereo. Tip = Hot/Left, Ring = Cold/Right, Sleeve = Ground.

+48V DC power sent from the mixer/preamp to condenser microphones over the same XLR cable that carries the audio signal. Required for condenser mics; does not harm dynamic mics (which simply ignore it).

The directional sensitivity of a microphone — the pattern describing where it picks up sound and where it rejects sound. Common patterns: cardioid (front), supercardioid (tighter front), omnidirectional (all directions), figure-8/bidirectional (front and back).
A microphone using a moving coil and magnet to convert sound to electrical signal. Rugged, no power required, handles high SPL well. Used for handheld, podium, and high-SPL applications.

A microphone using a charged diaphragm and backplate to convert sound to electrical signal. More sensitive and accurate than dynamic mics, especially at high frequencies. Requires phantom power (+48V) or battery. Used for ceiling arrays, boundary mics, and studio applications.

The angular spread of a speaker's sound output, measured at the points where SPL drops 6 dB from the on-axis level. Specified as horizontal × vertical (e.g., 90° × 60°). Determines how many speakers are needed to cover a listening area.

lessons.content:
THE AUDIO SIGNAL CHAIN

Every audio system follows the same fundamental signal flow:

Source → Preamplification → Processing → Amplification → Output

1. SOURCE: Microphones, media players, computers, Bluetooth receivers — anything that generates or provides an audio signal.

2. PREAMPLIFICATION: Mic-level signals are too weak for processing. A preamplifier (built into mixers, DSPs, or standalone units) boosts mic level to line level. This is where gain is set — too little gain creates noise; too much causes distortion.

3. PROCESSING: At line level, signals are mixed, equalized, compressed, routed, and otherwise manipulated. Modern AV systems use Digital Signal Processors (DSPs) that handle all processing in a single device.

4. AMPLIFICATION: Power amplifiers boost line-level signals to speaker level — enough voltage and current to physically move speaker drivers. Amplifier power is rated in watts.

5. OUTPUT: Speakers convert electrical energy back to acoustic energy (sound waves). The speaker is the final link between the system and the listener.

SIGNAL LEVELS

Three distinct signal levels exist in audio systems — mismatching them is a common source of problems:

Mic Level: -60 dBV to -40 dBV. The weakest signal. Output by microphones. Must be amplified to line level by a preamp. Sending mic level into a line-level input results in very quiet, noisy audio.

Line Level: There are two standards:
- Professional (+4 dBu): Used in commercial AV equipment
- Consumer (-10 dBV): Used in consumer electronics
The difference is approximately 12 dB. Connecting consumer equipment to professional inputs (or vice versa) causes level mismatches.

Speaker Level: The amplified output from a power amplifier. Much higher voltage than line level (tens of volts). NEVER connect speaker-level output to a mic or line input — it will damage equipment.

BALANCED VS. UNBALANCED

Balanced audio uses three conductors: hot (+), cold (-), and ground. The audio signal is carried on both the hot and cold wires, but the cold wire carries the signal inverted (opposite polarity). At the receiving end, the cold signal is flipped and added to the hot signal. Any electromagnetic interference picked up along the cable affects both wires equally — when the cold is flipped, the interference cancels out.

Balanced connections (XLR, TRS): Can run hundreds of feet without noise problems. Required for professional AV installations.

Unbalanced connections (RCA, TS): Signal on one wire, ground on the other. No noise cancellation. Maximum recommended run: 15-25 feet. Acceptable only for short connections between consumer equipment.

Rule: All permanent AV audio wiring should be balanced. Unbalanced connections are acceptable only for short patch cables in controlled environments.

MICROPHONE TYPES

Dynamic Microphones:
- How they work: Moving coil attached to a diaphragm moves within a magnetic field, generating electrical current
- Advantages: Rugged, no power needed, handles high SPL, relatively inexpensive
- Disadvantages: Less sensitivity, reduced high-frequency response compared to condensers
- Applications: Handheld wireless, podium, instruments, high-SPL environments

Condenser Microphones:
- How they work: Sound waves vibrate a thin diaphragm near a charged backplate, varying the capacitance and generating an electrical signal
- Advantages: Superior sensitivity and frequency response, excellent transient detail, available in very small form factors
- Disadvantages: Requires phantom power (+48V) or battery, more delicate, more susceptible to handling noise
- Applications: Ceiling microphone arrays, boundary/surface mics, lavalier/lapel mics, studio recording, measurement

Ribbon Microphones:
- Specialized type using a thin metal ribbon in a magnetic field
- Fragile and expensive — NOT common in commercial AV installations
- Typically bidirectional (figure-8) pattern
- NEVER apply phantom power to a ribbon microphone unless specifically rated for it — phantom power can destroy the ribbon element

POLAR PATTERNS

The polar pattern describes WHERE a microphone picks up sound:

Cardioid: Heart-shaped pattern. Picks up sound from the front, rejects sound from the rear. The most common pattern for presentations and speech. Good for isolating a single talker from background noise.

Supercardioid: Tighter pickup than cardioid with slightly more front reach, but has a small rear lobe of sensitivity. Better rejection of side noise but must be aimed more precisely. Common in conference table mics and shotgun-style mics.

Omnidirectional: Equal sensitivity in all directions (a sphere of pickup). Used for area coverage, ambient recording, and boundary microphones where the surface creates a half-omni pattern. Does not exhibit proximity effect.

Figure-8 (Bidirectional): Equal pickup from front and rear, strong rejection from sides. Used for face-to-face interviews and ribbon microphones. Rarely used in standard AV installations.

SPEAKER TYPES FOR AV

Ceiling Speakers: The most common speaker type in commercial AV. Installed in or on the ceiling for distributed audio coverage. Available in sizes from 4-inch to 8-inch drivers. Coverage angles typically 90° to 120° conical. Best for even coverage in meeting rooms, classrooms, and hallways.

Surface-Mount Speakers: Mounted on walls or ceilings in a box enclosure. Better low-frequency response than ceiling speakers. Common in bars, restaurants, retail, and spaces without drop ceilings. Available in various sizes and power ratings.

Column Array Speakers: Tall, slim vertical arrays that produce a narrow vertical pattern and wide horizontal pattern. Excellent speech intelligibility in reverberant spaces like worship halls, atriums, and gymnasiums. Sound drops only 3 dB per doubling of distance (vs. 6 dB for point sources).

Line Array Speakers: Large-format arrays for concerts, stadiums, and large venues. Multiple loudspeaker elements in a curved vertical array. Used in live sound and large-scale entertainment, not typical in corporate AV.

Subwoofers: Dedicated low-frequency speakers (below 80-120 Hz). Used when full-range bass reproduction is needed — entertainment, worship, and immersive environments. Not typically needed for speech-only systems.

COVERAGE ANGLE AND SPEAKER SPACING

A speaker's coverage angle determines how wide an area it covers. The -6 dB points define the edge of coverage — at those angles, the SPL is 6 dB lower than directly on-axis.

For ceiling speakers:
- Wider coverage angle (120°) = fewer speakers needed but less directional control
- Narrower coverage angle (60°-90°) = more speakers needed but better control and reduced ceiling bounce

Spacing rule of thumb: edge-to-edge coverage should overlap by approximately 50% to achieve the ±3 dB uniformity required by AVIXA A102.01.

scenarios.situation: During system commissioning, the audio from a wireless lavalier microphone has a low hum and buzzing noise.
scenarios.notice: Hum (60 Hz or 120 Hz) and buzz are typically caused by ground loops or unbalanced connections. Lavalier mics are inherently balanced, but the wireless receiver's output connection to the DSP might be unbalanced.
scenarios.nextStep: Check the cable from the wireless receiver to the DSP input. Verify it is a balanced connection (XLR or TRS) and that both the receiver and DSP are set for balanced operation. If the receiver only has unbalanced (RCA) output, use a DI box or balun to convert to balanced.
scenarios.whyMatters: Balanced vs. unbalanced connections and ground loop troubleshooting are tested on the CTS exam in both Domain 1 (design) and Domain 4 (service). Always use balanced connections in permanent installations.

scenarios.situation: A corporate client wants to add microphones to a conference table for a video conferencing system. The table seats 12 people in an oval configuration.
scenarios.notice: Conference table microphone coverage requires careful pattern selection. A single microphone will not cover all 12 seats adequately.
scenarios.nextStep: Recommend a ceiling microphone array (condenser, wide coverage) or multiple boundary microphones (condenser, surface-mount) on the table. For 12 people, typically 2-3 boundary microphones or a ceiling array with multiple pickup zones. Ensure the DSP has acoustic echo cancellation (AEC) for far-end audio.
scenarios.whyMatters: Microphone selection based on application is a Domain 1 topic. The CTS exam tests your ability to choose the right microphone type and quantity based on room configuration and use case.

lessons.examRelevance: Audio signal flow, signal levels, balanced vs. unbalanced, microphone types and patterns, and speaker selection appear across Domains 1, 2, and 4. Common exam questions: identifying the correct microphone type for a scenario, selecting balanced vs. unbalanced connections, understanding phantom power requirements, and matching speaker types to room applications.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which microphone type requires phantom power to operate?
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Condenser microphones require +48V phantom power (or battery power) to charge the backplate. Dynamic microphones generate their own signal through electromagnetic induction and do not need external power.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the primary advantage of balanced audio connections over unbalanced?
options: Balanced connections reject electromagnetic interference over long runs
Balanced connections carry higher signal levels
knowledgeCheck.answer: Balanced connections reject electromagnetic interference over long runs
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Balanced audio uses three conductors with the cold signal inverted. At the receiving end, interference picked up equally on both signal wires cancels out when the cold signal is flipped. This allows cable runs of hundreds of feet without noise.

memorize: Signal flow: Source → Preamp → Processing → Amplification → Output
Signal levels: Mic (-60 to -40 dBV), Pro Line (+4 dBu), Consumer Line (-10 dBV), Speaker (amplified)
XLR pins: 1=Ground, 2=Hot(+), 3=Cold(-)
Phantom power: +48V for condenser mics
Polar patterns: Cardioid (front), Supercardioid (tight front + small rear lobe), Omni (all), Figure-8 (front+back)
understand: Balanced cancels noise by inverting and summing — interference cancels because it is equal on both conductors
Dynamic mics are rugged and need no power; condensers are sensitive and need phantom power
Coverage angle determines how many speakers are needed — wider angle = fewer speakers but less control
practice: Draw the audio signal flow for a conference room with wireless mics, DSP, amplifier, and ceiling speakers
Match microphone types to applications: podium, conference table, ceiling, handheld
examTraps: NEVER apply phantom power to a ribbon mic (unless specifically rated for it) — it can destroy the element
Mic level into a line input = quiet and noisy, NOT loud and distorted
Supercardioid has a small REAR lobe — it does NOT reject all rear sound like cardioid does
studyNotes.fieldTip: When troubleshooting audio noise, check balanced/unbalanced connections first. Converting an unbalanced RCA output to balanced XLR with a proper DI box solves 80% of hum and buzz problems in the field.

lessons.summary: Audio signal flow moves from Source through Preamplification, Processing (DSP), Amplification, to Output (speakers). Three signal levels exist: mic level (weakest), line level (processing standard), and speaker level (amplified). Balanced connections (XLR/TRS) reject noise over long runs. Dynamic mics need no power; condensers require +48V phantom power. Polar patterns determine pickup directionality — cardioid is most common for speech. Speaker types include ceiling, surface-mount, and column array, each suited to specific applications.
